claim: C. elegans motor neurons have dendritic spines that are structurally defined by a dynamic actin cytoskeleton.
source: Here, we used super-resolution microscopy, electron microscopy, live-cell imaging and genetics to show that C. elegans motor neurons have functional dendritic spines that: (1) are structurally defined by a dynamic actin cytoskeleton
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from super-resolution microscopy showing LifeAct::GFP enrichment in spines, live imaging showing dynamic actin remodeling, and genetic experiments showing that actin regulators affect spine density.

claim: C. elegans motor neuron dendritic spines appose presynaptic dense projections.
source: Here, we used super-resolution microscopy, electron microscopy, live-cell imaging and genetics to show that C. elegans motor neurons have functional dendritic spines that: (1) are structurally defined by a dynamic actin cytoskeleton; (2) appose presynaptic dense projections
evidence: The claim is supported by EM reconstruction showing DD1 spines in direct apposition with presynaptic termini and Airyscan imaging showing RAB-3 clusters adjacent to spines.

claim: C. elegans motor neuron dendritic spines localize ER and ribosomes.
source: Here, we used super-resolution microscopy, electron microscopy, live-cell imaging and genetics to show that C. elegans motor neurons have functional dendritic spines that: (1) are structurally defined by a dynamic actin cytoskeleton; (2) appose presynaptic dense projections; (3) localize ER and ribosomes
evidence: The claim is supported by EM reconstruction detecting SER-like structures and ribosomes in DD1 spines, and light microscopy detecting ribosomal protein RPS-18::GFP in DD spines.

claim: C. elegans motor neuron dendritic spines display calcium transients triggered by presynaptic activity and propagated by internal Ca++ stores.
source: Here, we used super-resolution microscopy, electron microscopy, live-cell imaging and genetics to show that C. elegans motor neurons have functional dendritic spines that: (1) are structurally defined by a dynamic actin cytoskeleton; (2) appose presynaptic dense projections; (3) localize ER and ribosomes; (4) display calcium transients triggered by presynaptic activity and propagated by internal Ca++ stores
evidence: The claim is supported by GCaMP6s imaging showing spontaneous Ca++ transients in DD spines, optogenetic activation of VA neurons triggering Ca++ changes in DD spines, and ryanodine treatment blocking Ca++ propagation.

claim: C. elegans motor neuron dendritic spines respond to activity-dependent signals that regulate spine density.
source: Here, we used super-resolution microscopy, electron microscopy, live-cell imaging and genetics to show that C. elegans motor neurons have functional dendritic spines that: (1) are structurally defined by a dynamic actin cytoskeleton; (2) appose presynaptic dense projections; (3) localize ER and ribosomes; (4) display calcium transients triggered by presynaptic activity and propagated by internal Ca++ stores; (5) respond to activity-dependent signals that regulate spine density.
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments showing that reducing acetylcholine signaling decreases spine density, increasing acetylcholine levels elevates spine density, and optogenetic activation of cholinergic neurons increases spine density.

claim: Actin is enriched in DD spines compared to the dendritic shaft.
source: This representation shows a clear separation between measurements of cytosolic mCherry that is evenly distributed throughout dendrites (median spine/shaft ratio <1) versus that of the LifeAct::GFP signal (median spine/shaft ratio >1) (KS test, p<0.0001, Figure 1E). Thus, actin is enriched in DD spines.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements showing LifeAct::GFP has a spine/shaft ratio >1 while cytosolic mCherry has a ratio <1, with statistical significance (KS test, p<0.0001).

claim: Spine density measurements with cytoplasmic mCherry, LifeAct::GFP, and MYR::mRuby are not significantly different.
source: This interpretation is strengthened by our finding that independent measurements of the spine density (mean spine numbers/10 µm) with either cytoplasmic mCherry, LifeAct::GFP or the membrane bound marker, myristolated-mRuby (MYR::mRuby) are not significantly different (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative spine density measurements from multiple fluorescent markers showing no significant difference.

claim: DD motor neurons display predominantly thin/mushroom spines, with lesser fractions of filopodial, stubby and branched shapes.
source: By these criteria, adult DD neurons have predominantly thin/mushroom spines, with lesser fractions of filopodial, stubby and branched shapes (Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative classification of spine morphologies from Airyscan imaging showing thin/mushroom spines at 55.5 ± 14.5%, filopodial at 10.3 ± 8.7%, stubby at 18.8 ± 10.7%, and branched at 15.4 ± 6.0%.

claim: EM reconstruction of DD1 detected twelve DD1 spines with multiple morphological shapes.
source: Reconstruction of 50 nm serial ultrathin sections from the anterior DD1 dendrite detected twelve DD1 spines, with multiple morphological shapes (Figure 2C) that resemble classes revealed by fluorescent markers (Figure 1I; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-C).
evidence: The claim is supported by EM reconstruction data from serial sections of DD1 dendrite.

claim: Some DD spines can remodel in vivo.
source: Our live-imaging revealed that some DD spines can remodel in vivo (Video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data showing spine remodeling over time.

claim: Transient filopodial-like extensions from the dendritic shaft were observed in 11 out of 25 movies.
source: During imaging sessions of >30 min, we observed cases of transient filopodial-like extensions (11 out of 25 movies) from the dendritic shaft that retract in the course of minutes (Videos 2–3).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of live imaging movies.

claim: DD motor neurons display a dynamic actin cytoskeleton.
source: Live-imaging of DD motor neurons also detected a dynamic actin cytoskeleton (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-E and Videos 2–3), consistent with previous reports for mammalian dendritic spines (Honkura et al., 2008; Mikhaylova et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data showing fluctuations in LifeAct::GFP fluorescence over time, and is consistent with previous reports in mammalian systems.

claim: The Arp2/3 complex and two of its activators (TOCA-1 and Wave Regulatory Complex) are required to maintain DD spine density.
source: We found that the Arp2/3 complex, and two of its activators, the F-BAR protein TOCA-1 (Ho et al., 2004) and the Wave Regulatory Complex (Chen et al., 2010), are required to maintain DD spine density (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi experiments showing reduced spine density when these actin regulators are knocked down, with citations to previous work characterizing these proteins.

claim: TOCA-1 functions cell-autonomously in DD neurons to promote spine formation.
source: Restoring expression of TOCA-1 to DD neurons rescued the spine density defect (Figure 1—figure supplement 2G), demonstrating that actin polymerization is required cell-autonomously to promote spine formation.
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiments showing that DD-specific expression of TOCA-1 restores spine density in toca-1 mutants.

claim: Approximately 84% of DD spines are associated with at least one presynaptic cluster.
source: Among the 128 spines identified by LifeAct::GFP, most (~84%) reside near at least one presynaptic cluster (denoted 'contacted' in Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of Airyscan imaging showing RAB-3 clusters adjacent to DD spines.

claim: Approximately 40% of DD spines are associated with multiple presynaptic clusters of RAB-3 puncta.
source: Approximately ~40% (51/128) of DD spines are associated with multiple presynaptic clusters of RAB-3 puncta which suggests that individual spines receive input from >1 presynaptic terminal (arrowheads, Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of Airyscan imaging data.

claim: All twelve DD1 spines detected by EM reconstruction are in direct apposition with presynaptic termini of cholinergic motor neurons.
source: Our EM reconstruction of a segment of DD1 dendrite revealed 12 spines, all in direct apposition with the presynaptic termini of cholinergic motor neurons (VA1, VA2 and VB2) (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by EM reconstruction data.

claim: 84.8% of cholinergic presynaptic inputs in the reconstructed DD1 region appose DD1 spines.
source: Of the 33 cholinergic presynaptic inputs in this region, 84.8% (n = 28/33) appose DD1 spines, whereas only 15.2% (n = 5/33) are positioned along the dendritic shaft.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of EM reconstruction data.

claim: Two thirds of DD1 spines receive input from more than one neuron class.
source: Two thirds of DD1 spines (n = 8/12) receive input from more than one neuron class. That is, a single DD1 spine head is contacted by presynaptic termini of both VA and VB class cholinergic motor neurons (Figure 2C and Video 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of EM reconstruction data.

claim: ACR-12::GFP clusters are detected on approximately 95% of DD spines.
source: We detected ACR-12::GFP clusters on ~95% of DD spines (n = 121/127) (Figure 2F–G), with 68.5% (n = 87/127) localized at spine tips and the remainder either positioned along the lateral side of the spine (~12%, n = 15/127) or at both the side and tip (~15%, n = 19/127) (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of Airyscan imaging data.

claim: 43.3% of DD spines have more than one ACR-12::GFP cluster.
source: 43.3% of spines (n = 55/127) had more than one ACR-12::GFP cluster (Figure 2H), a finding that mirrors a recent observation that spines of mammalian cortical neurons can display multiple assemblages of the postsynaptic protein PSD-95 (Hruska et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of Airyscan imaging data and is consistent with findings in mammalian neurons.

claim: Endogenous LEV-10 is detected at 100% of DD spines using NATF labeling.
source: When GFP1-10 was selectively expressed in DD neurons from a transgenic array (i.e., Pflp-13::GFP1-10), we detected LEV-10 NATF-GFP signal at 100% (n = 159/159) of DD spines (Figure 2I–K), further substantiating the idea that DD spines are sites of presynaptic input.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of NATF labeling data.

claim: DD spines do not display electron dense postsynaptic densities (PSDs).
source: Our EM analysis confirmed that DD spines do not display electron dense postsynaptic densities (PSDs), a feature that is also not detected in electron micrographs of most C. elegans postsynaptic terminals (Lim et al., 2016; White et al., 1976; White et al., 1986; Zhen et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by EM analysis and is consistent with previous reports of C. elegans synapses.

claim: EM reconstruction of DD1 revealed cisternae SER-like structures in both the dendritic shaft and spines.
source: Our EM reconstruction of DD1 revealed cisternae SER-like structures in both the dendritic shaft and spines of DD1 (Figure 3A–B) and apparent ribosomes in some DD1 spines (Figure 3B'').
evidence: The claim is supported by EM reconstruction data.

claim: Ribosomal protein RPS-18::GFP is detected in about half (44.5 ± 12.0%) of DD spines.
source: Consistent with this observation are our light microscopy images that detect the ribosomal protein RPS-18::GFP (Noma et al., 2017) in about half of (44.5 ± 12.0%) DD spines (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of Airyscan imaging data and cites the source of the RPS-18::GFP marker.

claim: EM reconstruction did not find mitochondria or microtubules in all twelve DD spines.
source: Our EM reconstruction did not find mitochondria or microtubules in all twelve DD spines (Figure 3D), while both organelles were detected in the DD1 dendritic shaft (Video 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by EM reconstruction data.

claim: DD spines and shafts display spontaneous Ca++ transients that last for several seconds.
source: Live-imaging (at 2 s intervals) revealed spontaneous Ca++ transients in both DD spines and shafts that lasted for several seconds (Figure 4A–C and Video 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging data using GCaMP6s.

claim: Ca++ transients occur simultaneously in adjacent spines about 50% of the time.
source: Interestingly, Ca++ transients were observed simultaneously in adjacent spines about 50% of the time (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of GCaMP6s imaging data.

claim: The distribution of time differences between neighboring spine Ca++ peaks is statistically different from a uniform distribution.
source: To estimate the likelihood of simultaneous Ca++ peaks occurring by chance, we compared the distribution of the observed time differences between neighboring spine Ca++ peaks (△T) to that of a uniform distribution (at 2 s intervals) over the period of observation (20 s). These distributions are statistically different (KS test, p<0.0001), suggesting that Ca++ dynamics may reflect mechanisms for postsynaptic coordination of adjacent DD spine activity (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of GCaMP6s imaging data.

claim: Optogenetic activation of VA neurons with ceChrimson triggers correlated GCaMP6s fluorescence in DD spines.
source: ceChrimson was activated by a brief flash of 561 nm light (80 ms) at 2.5 s intervals and the GCaMP6s signal in DD neurons was recorded at 2 Hz. This experiment detected a correlation of GCaMP6s fluorescence with ceChrimson activation (Figure 4E–G and Videos 7–8).
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic experiments showing Ca++ changes in DD spines correlated with activation of presynaptic VA neurons.

claim: Local cholinergic release can trigger Ca++ changes in neighboring and distant spines.
source: Live imaging two seconds after ceChrimson activation detected elevated GCaMP signals in spines in all three regions that then waned with time (Figure 4J and Video 9). This observation suggests that local cholinergic release can trigger Ca++ changes in neighboring and distant spines.
evidence: The claim is supported by local optogenetic activation experiments showing Ca++ changes propagating to adjacent and distant spines.

claim: Blocking ryanodine receptor-dependent Ca++ release substantially attenuates Ca++ transients in all spines.
source: Because activation of intracellular Ca++ stores depends on ryanodine-sensitive channels, we repeated the local spine activation experiment (Figure 4I) in the presence of 1 mM ryanodine. Blocking ryanodine receptor-dependent Ca++ release substantially attenuated Ca++ transients in all spines (Figure 4K) thus suggesting that intracellular Ca++ is required to propagate the initial activation.
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological experiments using ryanodine treatment.

claim: A mutation that disrupts the UNC-68/Ryanodine receptor function results in substantially reduced intrinsic Ca++ dynamics in DD spines.
source: Further, a mutation that disrupts the UNC-68/Ryanodine receptor function results in substantially reduced intrinsic Ca++ dynamics in DD spines (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic experiments using unc-68 mutants.

claim: Spine density increases as DD neurons elongate during development from L3 to young adult stages.
source: LifeAct::GFP imaging in late larval to adult stages (L3, early L4, mid-L4 and young adult), revealed that spine density increases as DD neurons elongate during development (Figure 5B and E and S4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of spine density across developmental stages.

claim: Reduced acetylcholine release in the unc-17/vAChT mutant results in reduced DD spine density at the L4 larval stage.
source: Reduced acetylcholine release in the unc-17/vAChT mutant results in reduced DD spine density at the L4 larval stage (Figure 5C and E and S4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of spine density in unc-17 mutants.

claim: Increased acetylcholine levels in ace-1;ace-2 mutants result in precocious elevation of spine density during development.
source: In contrast, increased acetylcholine levels (i.e., in ace-1;ace-2 mutants) results in precocious elevation of spine density during development (Figure 5D and E and S4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of spine density in ace-1;ace-2 double mutants.

claim: The developmental elevation of spine density is blocked in unc-31/CAPS mutants.
source: The developmental elevation of spine density is also blocked in unc-31/CAPS mutants (Speese et al., 2007), in which neuropeptide and catecholamine neurotransmitter release is also prevented (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of spine density in unc-31 mutants and cites previous work characterizing this mutant.

claim: Animals grown in the presence of histamine to silence cholinergic neurons show reduced spine density at the L4 stage.
source: Animals grown in the presence of histamine showed reduced spine density at the L4 stage compared to animals grown on plates without histamine (Figure 5F–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments using histamine-gated chloride channels to reduce cholinergic activity.

claim: Optogenetic activation of A-class motor neurons during L2-L3 development leads to increased spine density in L3 larvae.
source: Animals were exposed to 561 nm light to activate ceChrimson for a brief period (1 s every 4 s) during the L2-L3 stage larval development (See Materials and methods). This treatment led to increased spine density (scored in L3 larvae) in comparison to animals without ceChrimson stimulation (Figure 5J–M).
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic experiments showing that temporal activation of cholinergic neurons increases spine density.

claim: VD-class GABAergic neurons display dendritic spines throughout the dorsal nerve cord.
source: This experiment confirmed the presence of dendritic spines in VD neurons throughout the dorsal nerve cord (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Airyscan imaging of VD neurons after DD ablation.

claim: EM reconstruction of 27 μm of the anterior VD2 dendrite detected nine dendritic spines.
source: Our EM reconstruction of 27 μm of the anterior VD2 dendrite detected nine dendritic spines (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by EM reconstruction data.

claim: Most VD spines are juxtaposed to presynaptic termini of cholinergic motor neurons (DA2, DB1, AS2).
source: Similar to DD1, most VD spines are juxtaposed to presynaptic termini of cholinergic motor neurons (DA2, DB1, AS2).
evidence: The claim is supported by EM reconstruction data showing VD spine contacts with cholinergic presynaptic termini.

claim: Dendritic spines were originally described by Ramon y Cajal.
source: These dendritic 'spines' were originally described by Ramon y Cajal (Yuste, 2015) and are now recognized as key functional components of neural circuits.
evidence: The claim cites a historical reference about the original description of dendritic spines.

claim: Spine morphology and density are regulated by neural activity in plastic responses that are strongly correlated with learning and memory.
source: For example, spine morphology and density are regulated by neural activity in plastic responses that are strongly correlated with learning and memory (Kozorovitskiy et al., 2005; Moser et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim cites previous studies showing correlation between spine plasticity and learning/memory.

claim: Spine-like protrusions have been reported for invertebrate neurons.
source: Although spine-like protrusions have been reported for invertebrate neurons (Leiss, 2008; Petralia et al., 2016), few studies (Bushey et al., 2011; Scott et al., 2003) have rigorously determined if these structures share functional features with vertebrate spines.
evidence: The claim cites previous reports of spine-like structures in invertebrates.

claim: The anatomy of the C. elegans nervous system was originally defined by reconstruction of electron micrographs of serial sections.
source: The anatomy of the C. elegans nervous system was originally defined by reconstruction of electron micrographs (EM) of serial sections. This approach revealed that a small subset of neurons displays short, spine-like protrusions. These include five classes of motor neurons (RMD, RME, SMD, DD, VD) and an interneuron (RIP) (White et al., 1976; White et al., 1986).
evidence: The claim cites the original EM reconstruction studies of the C. elegans nervous system.

claim: Light and electron microscopy detected similar dendritic protrusions extending from motor neurons in the nematode Ascaris.
source: Light and electron microscopy detected similar dendritic protrusions extending from motor neurons in the nematode, Ascaris (Angstadt et al., 1989; Stretton et al., 1978).
evidence: The claim cites previous studies detecting dendritic protrusions in Ascaris.

claim: Recent reports used light microscopy to show that a postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor is localized near the tips of spine-like protrusions on DD class motor neurons that directly appose presynaptic termini.
source: Finally, recent reports used light microscopy to show that a postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor is localized near the tips of spine-like protrusions on the DD class motor neurons that directly appose presynaptic termini (Oliver et al., 2018; Philbrook et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim cites recent studies showing acetylcholine receptor localization at DD spine tips.

claim: The actin cytoskeleton is a structural hallmark of vertebrate dendritic spines.
source: Because the actin cytoskeleton is a structural hallmark of vertebrate dendritic spines (Cingolani and Goda, 2008), we also labeled DD neurons with the actin marker, LifeAct::GFP (Riedl et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim cites established knowledge about actin in vertebrate spines and the source of the LifeAct marker.

claim: EM reconstruction of mammalian dendritic spines in the hippocampus revealed that thin and mushroom shapes predominate.
source: EM reconstruction of mammalian dendritic spines in the hippocampus also revealed that thin and mushroom shapes predominate (Harris and Stevens, 1989; Harris et al., 1992) and that filopodial and stubby spines are less abundant (Fiala et al., 1998; Zuo et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim cites previous EM studies of mammalian spine morphology.

claim: A similarly heterogeneous array of spine shapes among mammalian neurons has been attributed to active remodeling of spine architecture.
source: Although we have assigned DD motor neuron spines to four discrete classifications, both fluorescence imaging and EM reconstruction point to a broader array of spine types that includes potential intermediate forms (Figure 1G–H; 2C). A similarly heterogeneous array of spine shapes among mammalian neurons has been attributed to active remodeling of spine architecture (Sala and Segal, 2014; Zuo et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim cites previous studies attributing heterogeneous spine shapes to active remodeling.

claim: In the mature mammalian cortex, extended imaging has revealed transient filopodial extensions with a lifetime shorter than a day, and potential plasticity over longer intervals, where approximately half of spines are stable for months.
source: In the mature mammalian cortex, extended imaging has revealed transient filopodial extensions with a lifetime shorter than a day, and potential plasticity over longer intervals, where approximately half of spines are stable for months (Trachtenberg et al., 2002; Zuo et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim cites previous studies of spine dynamics in mammalian cortex.

claim: Disruption of the Arp2/3 complex or its activators has been previously shown to reduce dendritic spine density in the mammalian brain and to impair function.
source: Disruption of the Arp2/3 complex or its activators has been previously shown to reduce dendritic spine density in the mammalian brain and to impair function (Kim et al., 2013; Lippi et al., 2011; Soderling et al., 2003; Spence et al., 2016; Westphal et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim cites multiple previous studies showing effects of Arp2/3 disruption on mammalian spine density.

claim: Functional dendritic spines are sites of presynaptic input.
source: Because functional dendritic spines are sites of presynaptic input (Alvarez and Sabatini, 2007; Hering and Sheng, 2001; Petralia et al., 2016), we investigated the disposition of DD spines vis-a-vis their main presynaptic partners, the cholinergic VA and VB class motor neurons (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim cites established knowledge about dendritic spines being sites of presynaptic input.

claim: Individual spines on GABAergic neurons in the mammalian hippocampus can have inputs from multiple presynaptic termini.
source: We note that individual spines on GABAergic neurons in the mammalian hippocampus can also have inputs from multiple presynaptic termini (Acsády et al., 1998; Gulyás et al., 1992; Petralia et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim cites previous studies showing multiple inputs to individual spines in mammalian hippocampus.

claim: Robustly stained PSDs are observed at vertebrate glutamatergic synapses, but PSDs are either absent or much less prominent in electron micrographs of vertebrate synapses at spines for other neurotransmitters (glycine, GABA, acetylcholine).
source: Although robustly stained PSDs are observed at vertebrate glutamatergic synapses, PSDs are either absent or much less prominent in electron micrographs of vertebrate synapses at spines for other neurotransmitters (glycine, GABA, acetylcholine) (Knott et al., 2002; Kubota et al., 2007; Umbriaco et al., 1994).
evidence: The claim cites previous studies showing differences in PSD staining at different types of vertebrate synapses.

claim: Key cytoplasmic organelles such as Smooth Endoplasmic Reticulum (SER) are present in both dendritic shafts and spines of mammalian neurons.
source: Key cytoplasmic organelles such as Smooth Endoplasmic Reticulum (SER), are present in both dendritic shafts and spines of mammalian neurons (Harris and Stevens, 1989).
evidence: The claim cites previous studies showing SER in mammalian dendritic spines.

claim: Spine SER regulates activity-dependent Ca++ release through the ryanodine receptor.
source: In addition to its role of processing membrane proteins, spine SER regulates activity-dependent Ca++ release through the ryanodine receptor (Fill and Copello, 2002).
evidence: The claim cites previous work on the role of SER in Ca++ release.

claim: Polysomes and rough ER have been reported in spines, consistent with the possibility of local translation at synapses.
source: Other structures such as polysomes and rough ER have also been reported in spines, consistent with the possibility of local translation at synapses (Bourne and Harris, 2008; Hafner et al., 2019; Nimchinsky et al., 2002; Steward and Reeves, 1988).
evidence: The claim cites previous studies reporting polysomes and rough ER in spines.

claim: Mitochondria and microtubules are reported to be rare in the dendritic spines of mature mammalian neurons.
source: Mitochondria and microtubules are reported to be rare in the dendritic spines of mature mammalian neurons (Bourne and Harris, 2008; Nimchinsky et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim cites previous reports about the rarity of mitochondria and microtubules in mammalian spines.

claim: Ca++ is a key signaling molecule to mediate activity-dependent synaptic plasticity.
source: Ca++ is a key signaling molecule to mediate activity-dependent synaptic plasticity (Lee et al., 2016; Rochefort and Konnerth, 2012).
evidence: The claim cites established knowledge about the role of Ca++ in synaptic plasticity.

claim: Muscle cells that share cholinergic input with DD spines display prolonged elevation of Ca++ over a period of seconds.
source: Muscle cells that share cholinergic input with DD spines also display prolonged elevation of Ca++ over a period of seconds (Liu et al., 2013), suggesting that cholinergic neurons regulate the long lasting bursts of Ca++ in spines and muscle cells.
evidence: The claim cites a previous study showing Ca++ dynamics in muscle cells receiving cholinergic input.

claim: A similar explanation of convergent input was proposed for the coordinated firing of adjacent dendritic spines in rat hippocampal neurons.
source: A similar explanation of convergent input was proposed for the coordinated firing of adjacent dendritic spines in rat hippocampal neurons (Takahashi et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim cites a previous study proposing convergent input as an explanation for coordinated spine activity.

claim: In developing hippocampal neurons, an initial Ca++ transient can be propagated to neighboring spines via Ca++ release from intracellular stores.
source: In developing hippocampal neurons, an initial Ca++ transient can be propagated to neighboring spines via Ca++ release from intracellular stores (Lee et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim cites a previous study showing Ca++ propagation in hippocampal neurons.

claim: In hippocampal neurons, local glutamate uncaging triggers ryanodine-insensitive Ca++ transients in the excited spine but this effect is rapid (~250 ms).
source: In hippocampal neurons, local glutamate uncaging triggers ryanodine-insensitive Ca++ transients in the excited spine but this effect is rapid (~250 ms) (Lee et al., 2016) and thus a similar rapid initial Ca++ transient might have been missed by our experimental set up that detects GCaMP signals ~ 2 s after ceChrimson activation (Figure 4K).
evidence: The claim cites a previous study showing rapid Ca++ transients in hippocampal neurons and uses this to interpret the current experimental results.

claim: Spine shape and density are modulated throughout development in mammalian neurons.
source: In mammalian neurons, spine shape and density are modulated throughout development (Fiala et al., 1998; Harris et al., 1992; Kanjhan et al., 2016a).
evidence: The claim cites previous studies showing developmental modulation of spine morphology in mammals.

claim: Dendritic spines can be modulated by changes in synaptic strength.
source: Dendritic spines can be modulated by changes in synaptic strength (Bourne and Harris, 2008; Nimchinsky et al., 2002; Rochefort and Konnerth, 2012).
evidence: The claim cites established knowledge about spine modulation by synaptic strength.

claim: Long-term potentiation is correlated with increased numbers of spines in the mammalian brain.
source: Long-term potentiation is correlated with increased numbers of spines in the mammalian brain (Engert and Bonhoeffer, 1999; Trachtenberg et al., 2002; Holtmaat et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim cites previous studies showing correlation between LTP and spine density.

claim: Hyperactivity is associated with increased dendritic spine density in hypoglossal motor neurons.
source: Similarly, hyperactivity is associated with increased dendritic spine density in hypoglossal motor neurons (Kanjhan et al., 2016b).
evidence: The claim cites a previous study showing activity-dependent spine density changes in motor neurons.

claim: Long-term depression induces spine shrinkage and may lead to spine elimination.
source: Conversely, long-term depression induces spine shrinkage (Zhou et al., 2004) and may lead to their elimination (Hasegawa et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim cites previous studies showing effects of LTD on spine morphology.

claim: The prevalence of postsynaptic protrusions in vertebrate and invertebrate nervous systems suggests that spines are ancient structures.
source: The prevalence of postsynaptic protrusions in vertebrate and invertebrate nervous systems suggests that spines are ancient structures and thus could be effectively investigated in a variety of model organisms (Leiss, 2008; Petralia et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the widespread presence of spine-like structures across species, with citations to reviews discussing this.

claim: C. elegans is transparent, so live imaging does not require surgery or other invasive methods that are typically necessary for in vivo imaging of spines in an intact mammalian nervous system.
source: Because C. elegans is transparent, live imaging does not require surgery or other invasive methods that are typically necessary for in vivo imaging of spines in an intact mammalian nervous system.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about C. elegans transparency and the requirements for mammalian in vivo imaging.

claim: A recent study reported that neurexin is necessary for spine morphogenesis in DDs, and in this case, neuroligin is not required.
source: A recent study, for example, reported that neurexin, a conserved membrane protein and established regulator of synaptic assembly, is necessary for spine morphogenesis in DDs. Interestingly, in this case, neuroligin, the canonical neurexin ligand, is not required, suggesting a potentially new neurexin-dependent mechanism of synaptogenesis (Oliver et al., 2018; Philbrook et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim cites recent studies showing neurexin's role in DD spine morphogenesis.

claim: Other neurons reported to have 'short branches' in the original EM reconstruction of the adult C. elegans are likely to display bona fide dendritic spines.
source: Thus, other neurons reported to have 'short branches' in the original EM reconstruction of the adult C. elegans (White et al., 1986), the cholinergic (RMD, SMD) and GABAergic (RME) motor neurons and the interneuron (RIP), are likely to display bona fide dendritic spines.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the current findings and previous EM observations, with citation to the original EM reconstruction.

claim: A developmentally regulated remodeling program transforms presynaptic boutons into postsynaptic spines in larval DD neurons.
source: Finally, a developmentally regulated remodeling program (Kurup and Jin, 2016; Petersen et al., 2011; White et al., 1978) transforms presynaptic boutons into postsynaptic spines in larval DD neurons and thus could be especially useful for live imaging studies of synaptic plasticity and spine morphogenesis.
evidence: The claim cites previous studies describing the DD remodeling program.

claim: In the adult, Dorsal D (DD) class GABAergic motor neurons extend axons to innervate dorsal muscles and receive cholinergic input at ventral dendrites.
source: In the adult, Dorsal D (DD) class GABAergic motor neurons extend axons to innervate dorsal muscles and receive cholinergic input at ventral dendrites (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by the schematic in Figure 1A showing DD neuron anatomy.

claim: Airyscan imaging is a type of super-resolution microscopy.
source: We used Airyscan imaging, a type of super-resolution microscopy (Korobchevskaya et al., 2017), to detect spine-like projections on the ventral processes of adult DD neurons labeled with a cytosolic mCherry marker (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim cites a reference describing Airyscan as a super-resolution technique.

claim: LifeAct::GFP is an actin marker.
source: Because the actin cytoskeleton is a structural hallmark of vertebrate dendritic spines (Cingolani and Goda, 2008), we also labeled DD neurons with the actin marker, LifeAct::GFP (Riedl et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim cites the original publication describing LifeAct::GFP as an actin marker.

claim: High Pressure Freezing (HPF) avoids potential artifacts arising from chemical fixation.
source: For this experiment, young adult animals were prepared using High Pressure Freezing (HPF) to avoid potential artifacts arising from chemical fixation (Mulcahy et al., 2018; Weimer et al., 2006; White et al., 1986).
evidence: The claim cites previous studies supporting the use of HPF to avoid fixation artifacts.

claim: The acetylcholine receptor (AChR) subunit ACR-12 is postsynaptic to cholinergic inputs at GABAergic motor neurons.
source: The acetylcholine receptor (AChR) subunit ACR-12 is postsynaptic to cholinergic inputs at GABAergic motor neurons (Petrash et al., 2013), and has been previously shown to localize to DD1 dendritic protrusions (Figure 2E) (He et al., 2015; Philbrook et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim cites previous studies characterizing ACR-12 localization.

claim: NATF (Native and Tissue-Specific Fluorescence) relies on the reconstitution of superfolder GFP (sfGFP) from the split-sfGFP fragments, GFP1-10 and GFP11.
source: NATF (Native and Tissue-Specific Fluorescence) relies on the reconstitution of superfolder GFP (sfGFP) from the split-sfGFP fragments, GFP1-10 and GFP11 (He et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim cites the publication describing the NATF method.

claim: LEV-10 is a co-factor protein of the acetylcholine receptor complex.
source: To obviate the possibility that localization of ACR-12::GFP clusters to DD spines results from over-expression, we used a new live-cell labeling scheme to detect an endogenous component of the acetylcholine receptor complex, the co-factor protein LEV-10 (Gally et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim cites a previous study characterizing LEV-10 as a co-factor of the acetylcholine receptor.

claim: Most C. elegans postsynaptic terminals do not display electron dense postsynaptic densities in electron micrographs.
source: Our EM analysis confirmed that DD spines do not display electron dense postsynaptic densities (PSDs), a feature that is also not detected in electron micrographs of most C. elegans postsynaptic terminals (Lim et al., 2016; White et al., 1976; White et al., 1986; Zhen et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim cites multiple previous EM studies of C. elegans synapses.

claim: Postsynaptic assemblages at non-glutamatergic synapses likely comprise distinct sets of scaffolding proteins, some of which are readily stained by heavy atoms used for EM imaging of glutamatergic synapses.
source: Postsynaptic assemblages at these synapses likely comprise distinct sets of scaffolding proteins, some of which are readily stained by heavy atoms used for EM imaging of glutamatergic synapses (Petralia et al., 2005; Petralia et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on cited studies about postsynaptic protein composition at different synapse types.

claim: The original EM reconstruction of the C. elegans nervous system detected spine-like structures on VD neurons.
source: In the adult C. elegans motor circuit, dendrites of the DD-class GABAergic motor neurons receive cholinergic input in the ventral nerve cord, whereas the VD class receives input in the dorsal nerve cord (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A). Because the original EM reconstruction of the C. elegans nervous system detected spine-like structures on VD neurons (White et al., 1976), we sought to verify this finding by using the LifeAct::GFP marker for Airyscan imaging.
evidence: The claim cites the original EM reconstruction study.

claim: Both the DD and VD classes of ventral cord GABAergic motor neurons display dendritic spines.
source: Thus, both the DD and VD classes of ventral cord GABAergic motor neurons display dendritic spines (White et al., 1976; White et al., 1986).
evidence: The claim is supported by the current study's data and cites the original EM reconstruction studies.

claim: Only 10% of excitatory synapses in the mature mammalian cortex are positioned on dendritic processes.
source: This finding parallels the observation that only 10% of excitatory synapses in the mature mammalian cortex are positioned on dendritic processes (Cingolani and Goda, 2008).
evidence: The claim cites a previous study about synapse distribution in mammalian cortex.

claim: The majority of DD1 spines (9/12) are postsynaptic to the same cholinergic motor neuron VA2.
source: For example, the majority of DD1 spines (9/12) are postsynaptic to the same cholinergic motor neuron VA2 (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of EM reconstruction data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Spines of mammalian cortical neurons can display multiple assemblages of the postsynaptic protein PSD-95.
source: 43.3% of spines (n = 55/127) had more than one ACR-12::GFP cluster (Figure 2H), a finding that mirrors a recent observation that spines of mammalian cortical neurons can display multiple assemblages of the postsynaptic protein PSD-95 (Hruska et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim cites a recent study showing multiple PSD-95 assemblages in mammalian spines.

claim: Six DD motor neurons are located in the C. elegans ventral nerve cord.
source: Six DD motor neurons are located in the C. elegans ventral nerve cord.
evidence: The claim is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1A and represents established anatomical knowledge.

claim: In the adult, DD presynaptic boutons innervate dorsal muscles and DD postsynaptic termini (spines) receive cholinergic input from VA and VB motor neurons on the ventral side.
source: In the adult, DD presynaptic boutons (oblong ovals) innervate dorsal muscles (gray cells) and DD postsynaptic termini (spines) receive cholinergic input from VA and VB motor neurons on the ventral side (magenta).
evidence: The claim is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1A and represents established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Spine density of young adults revealed by mCherry is 3.68 ± 0.8 spines/10 µm.
source: Spine density of young adults revealed by mCherry (3.68 ± 0.8 spines/10 µm) or LifeAct::GFP (3.43 ± 1.2 spines/10 µm) is not significantly different (t test, p=0.0855, n > 16 worms).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements reported in the text.

claim: Spine density of young adults revealed by LifeAct::GFP is 3.43 ± 1.2 spines/10 µm.
source: Spine density of young adults revealed by mCherry (3.68 ± 0.8 spines/10 µm) or LifeAct::GFP (3.43 ± 1.2 spines/10 µm) is not significantly different (t test, p=0.0855, n > 16 worms).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements reported in the text.

claim: Adult DD motor neurons have 55.5 ± 14.5% thin/mushroom spines, 10.3 ± 8.70% filopodial spines, 18.8 ± 10.4% stubby spines, and 15.4 ± 6.0% branched spines.
source: LifeAct::GFP reveals 1. Thin/Mushroom (55.5 ± 14.5%), 2. Filopodial (10.3 ± 8.70%), 3. Stubby (18.8 ± 10.4%), 4. Branched spines (15.4 ± 6.0%) in adult DD motor neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative classification of spine morphologies from imaging data.

claim: Spine density determined by 3D EM reconstruction of DD1 is 4.2 spines/10 µm.
source: Spine densities determined from young adult DD neurons labeled with mCherry (3.68 ± 0.8 spines/10 µm), LifeAct::GFP (3.43 ± 1.2spines/10 µm) and MYR::mRuby (3.09 ± 0.8 spines/10 µm) are not significantly different and are comparable to spine density determined by 3D EM reconstruction of DD1 (4.2 spines/10 µm) (dashed blue line).
evidence: The claim is supported by EM reconstruction data.

claim: Spine density of young adults revealed by MYR::mRuby is 3.09 ± 0.8 spines/10 µm.
source: Spine densities determined from young adult DD neurons labeled with mCherry (3.68 ± 0.8 spines/10 µm), LifeAct::GFP (3.43 ± 1.2spines/10 µm) and MYR::mRuby (3.09 ± 0.8 spines/10 µm) are not significantly different and are comparable to spine density determined by 3D EM reconstruction of DD1 (4.2 spines/10 µm) (dashed blue line).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements from imaging data.

claim: Wild-type young adults show 3.53 ± 1.0 spines/10 µm vs toca-1(tm2056) with 2.77 ± 1.1 spines/10 µm (t test, p<0.001).
source: WT young adults show 3.53 ± 1.0 spines/10 µm vs toca-1 (tm2056) with 2.77 ± 1.1 spines/10 µm (t test, *** is p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements comparing wild-type and mutant animals.

claim: Spine density is reduced with RNAi of wave/wve-1 (2.24 ± 0.7 spines/10 µm) or p21/arx-5 RNAi (2.20 ± 0.7 spines/10 µm) versus Empty Vector control (2.9 ± 0.4 spines/10 µm).
source: Spine density is reduced with RNAi of wave/wve-1 (2.24 ± 0.7 spines/10 µm) or p21/arx-5 RNAi (2.20 ± 0.7 spines/10 µm) versus Empty Vector (E.V.) control (2.9 ± 0.4 spines/10 µm). One-way ANOVA with Dunnett's multiple comparison test, ** is p<0.01, n > 9 worms.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements from RNAi experiments.

claim: TOCA-1a expression in DD neurons rescues the spine density defect in toca-1(tm2056) mutants (3.05 ± 0.8 spines/10 µm).
source: wild-type young adults show 3.53 ± 1.0 spines/10 µm vs 2.35 ± 0.9 spines/10 µm in toca-1(tm2056), which is rescued with TOCA-1a expression in DD neurons (Pflp-13::TOCA-1a::mCherry)=3.05 ± 0.8 spines/10 µm.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements from rescue experiments.

claim: 84.1 ± 6.4% of DD spines are contacted by cholinergic presynaptic sites as detected by Airyscan imaging.
source: Frequency of spines contacted by cholinergic presynaptic sites detected by Airyscan imaging (contacted, 84.1 ± 6.4% vs not contacted, 15.8 ± 6.4%, n = 128 spines from seven worms) or by EM (contacted, 100% vs not contacted, 0%, n = 12 spines from one worm).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of Airyscan imaging data.

claim: 100% of DD spines are contacted by cholinergic presynaptic sites as detected by EM.
source: Frequency of spines contacted by cholinergic presynaptic sites detected by Airyscan imaging (contacted, 84.1 ± 6.4% vs not contacted, 15.8 ± 6.4%, n = 128 spines from seven worms) or by EM (contacted, 100% vs not contacted, 0%, n = 12 spines from one worm).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of EM reconstruction data.

claim: 68.5% of ACR-12::GFP clusters are localized at spine tips.
source: We detected ACR-12::GFP clusters on ~95% of DD spines (n = 121/127) (Figure 2F–G), with 68.5% (n = 87/127) localized at spine tips and the remainder either positioned along the lateral side of the spine (~12%, n = 15/127) or at both the side and tip (~15%, n = 19/127) (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of ACR-12::GFP localization.

claim: Approximately 12% of ACR-12::GFP clusters are positioned along the lateral side of the spine.
source: We detected ACR-12::GFP clusters on ~95% of DD spines (n = 121/127) (Figure 2F–G), with 68.5% (n = 87/127) localized at spine tips and the remainder either positioned along the lateral side of the spine (~12%, n = 15/127) or at both the side and tip (~15%, n = 19/127) (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of ACR-12::GFP localization.

claim: Approximately 15% of ACR-12::GFP clusters are positioned at both the side and tip of spines.
source: We detected ACR-12::GFP clusters on ~95% of DD spines (n = 121/127) (Figure 2F–G), with 68.5% (n = 87/127) localized at spine tips and the remainder either positioned along the lateral side of the spine (~12%, n = 15/127) or at both the side and tip (~15%, n = 19/127) (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of ACR-12::GFP localization.

claim: VD spine density is 3.01 ± 1.43 spines/10 µm as measured by Airyscan imaging.
source: VD spine density (3.01 ± 1.43 spines/10 µm), n = 17.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements from Airyscan imaging.

claim: VD2 spine density detected by 3D EM is 3.33 spines/10 µm.
source: Dashed blue line represents spine density detected in VD2 with 3D EM (3.33 spines/10 µm).
evidence: The claim is supported by EM reconstruction data.

claim: 50.0% of DA and DB inputs are adjacent to VD spines.
source: 50.0% (n = 11/22) of DA and DB inputs are adjacent to VD spines.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of EM reconstruction data.

claim: DD spine density at the L4 stage is reduced by growth on histamine (2.58 ± 0.6) vs control (3.49 ± 0.9).
source: DD spine density at the L4 stage is reduced by growth on histamine (2.58 ± 0.6) vs control (3.49 ± 0.9). T-test, **=p < 0.01, n > 17.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements from histamine treatment experiments.

claim: Exposure to red-light for 6 hr elevates spine density at the L3 stage (3.9 ± 0.8) vs control (2.59 ± 0.8).
source: Exposure to red-light for 6 hr elevates spine density at the L3 stage (3.9 ± 0.8) vs control (2.59 ± 0.8). T-test, *** is p<0.001, n > 10.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements from optogenetic activation experiments.
